standard.title: Classification of Matter
standard.description: classify matter as elements, compounds or mixtures and compare different representations of these, including 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional models, symbols for elements and formulas for molecules and compounds
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can examine properties of natural and made materials and describe how these properties influence their use (AC9S4U04). They can describe physical changes and some chemical change indicators (AC9S8U07 — same band). They have not yet classified matter at the atomic/molecular level or used symbolic representations (symbols, formulas) to represent matter.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students classify matter as elements, compounds or mixtures — including sub-types of mixtures (solutions, suspensions, colloids) — use element symbols and molecular formulas to represent substances, and evaluate the strengths and limitations of different representations of matter.

nodes.label: Matter is classified as elements, compounds or mixtures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can classify a given substance as an element, compound or mixture, explain the basis for the classification at the atomic/molecular level, and distinguish between sub-types of mixtures.
nodes.minimum_width: Students classify at least five substances correctly as elements, compounds or mixtures and explain the basis for each classification in terms of the types of atoms or molecules present.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the classification hierarchy — elements (one type of atom), compounds (two or more elements chemically bonded), mixtures (two or more substances not chemically bonded) — and distinguish between mixture types (solutions, suspensions, colloids) using particle-level reasoning.
wider: Examine how Mendeleev arranged elements in the first periodic table and compare his arrangement with the current version — exploring what criteria changed as knowledge of atomic structure developed (AC9S8H01)

Create a timeline showing how the concept of an element has changed from ancient philosophy (Democritus) through Dalton's atomic theory to the modern model — tracing how the definition was refined by new evidence
Investigate how the classification of matter as elements, compounds and mixtures is used in industrial contexts — e.g. how mining separates mixed ores to extract pure elements or compounds
nodes.hinge_reason: Compound/mixture conflation is definitional — it directly produces errors in Node 2 formula work (writing formulas for mixtures, misattributing bonding) and Node 3 representation comparison (choosing the wrong representation type for a given substance). Students who have not resolved this at the atomic level cannot correctly interpret what a formula communicates.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate compounds and mixtures — both contain more than one substance — without understanding that the distinction is whether the components are chemically bonded. Making the atomic-level logic explicit (same type of atom = element; different atoms chemically bonded = compound; substances physically mixed = mixture) provides the reasoning foundation for all subsequent classification work.

success_criteria: Classifies at least five substances as elements, compounds or mixtures with atomic/molecular reasoning
Distinguishes between a compound and a mixture using particle-level explanation

nodes.label: Symbols and formulas represent elements and compounds
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use element symbols to identify elements from the periodic table, write and interpret molecular formulas for simple compounds, and explain what information a formula conveys about a compound's composition.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least eight elements by symbol from the periodic table and write or interpret formulas for at least three simple compounds, explaining what each formula conveys.
nodes.typical_width: Students use element symbols and molecular formulas to represent and interpret substances, explain why standardised symbols are used (universal communication), and identify the information conveyed by a formula (which elements, how many atoms of each) — distinguishing this from what a formula does not show (structure, arrangement).
wider: Examine how different representations convey different information — atomic symbol (element identity), molecular formula (composition), structural formula (bonding arrangement), 3D model (shape) — and identify which representation is most useful for different purposes
Research why some element symbols derive from Latin names (Fe, Au, Na, Pb) — connecting chemical convention history to the development of the periodic table
Explore how mixture percentages are used to represent composition in everyday contexts (alloy compositions, solution concentrations) and compare with formula representation
nodes.hinge_reason: Formula reading precision is a direct prerequisite for Node 3 representation comparison. Students who misread formulas — confusing atom counts with element counts, conflating H₂O₂ with H₂O — cannot meaningfully evaluate what different representations show or omit, because they cannot accurately read the most basic representation type.

response_modes.reason: Symbol and formula reading requires precision — misreading H₂O₂ as H₂O, or confusing atom counts with element counts, produces systematic errors that affect all subsequent chemistry work. Deliberate accurate practice with a range of formulas, combined with explanation of what each formula means, is more productive than breadth of chemical contexts at this stage.

success_criteria: Identifies at least eight elements by their chemical symbol
Writes or interprets formulas for at least three simple compounds, correctly identifying the elements present and the number of atoms of each

nodes.label: Representations model matter at different scales
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare 2D and 3D representations of elements and compounds — identifying what each representation shows and what it simplifies — and select the most appropriate representation for a given purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Students compare at least two representations of the same substance (e.g. symbol, formula, 2D diagram, 3D model) and explain what each one shows about the substance's composition.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the information conveyed by different representation types — chemical symbols, formulas, 2D dot diagrams, 3D ball-and-stick models, space-filling models — identify the strengths and limitations of each, and select the most appropriate representation for a given purpose.
wider: Use virtual and physical models to distinguish between elements and compounds in terms of types and arrangements of atoms — examining how the model makes the abstract atomic level visible
Construct representations of both physical and chemical changes and explain how the representation shows what has or hasn't changed at the particle level (connects to AC9S8U07)
Examine how computational molecular modelling is used in drug design and materials science — connecting representation of matter to real-world chemical research applications

response_modes.reason: Students tend to treat models as pictures of molecules rather than as representations that encode specific information about composition, bonding and structure. Comparing representations that convey different information — and explaining what each adds and what it omits — develops a more general understanding of representation as a tool in chemistry.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The representation-comparison direction develops genuine analytical thinking about models and their limitations — a transferable capability across all of science, not just chemistry. The computational modelling direction provides a contemporary research context that connects classroom models to real scientific practice.
success_criteria: Compares at least two representations of the same substance and explains what each shows about composition
Identifies at least one strength and one limitation of a named representation type
